Wasn't it just yesterday, or maybe the day before, that someone asked about the Times of London crossword puzzles, which are cryptics?  The theme clues here are similar to those, in which there are signal words that tell you that you need to reverse or scramble something, and all the words in these clues fall into that category.

But the British cryptics work just a little differently.  For one, the clues contain a "straight" part, too, and also the cue to reverse the word is in the clue, not the answer.  In other words, oddly enough, the reverse of what's going on here.

If my explanation seems dense, here's an example, using the first theme answer:

In cryptics, the clue might be [Taps a counterargument].  And the answer would be SPAT.  Here, "counter" tells you reverse something.  "Argument" is the "straight" clue.  "Taps" is what you have to reverse.

In British cryptics, you have to decipher which part of the clue serves which purpose.  Also, every other letter has no cross, so there are blocks (black squares) at least every other square.  So you get much less help if you're stuck.

Those who have seen these kinds of clues would find this puzzle fairly easy.  But those who haven't would be quite befuddled.

A thought on Faradays vs. coulombs, after much memory searching.

In electrochemistry, two chemical reactions occur, one releasing an electron, which travels through a wire, and the other takes that electron from the wire, and undergoes another chemical reaction.

For example, a very simple battery might have this reaction going at the anode:  [(aq) signifies "aqueous solution"]

       Li(s) -> Li+(aq)  +  e-          (Lithium atom gives up an electron)

And the cathode reaction might be 

   Ag+(aq)  +  e-  -->  Ag(s)        (Ag+ cation picks up an electron)

We might talk abut the amount of solid Ag produced as some number of moles**.  Ok, so in order to make that number of moles of Ag(s) we'd need a mole of electrons, or a *Faraday* of electrons.

** A mole is about 6.02 x 10^23 of something (602,000,000,000,000,000,000,000)  just like a dozen of something is 12 of something.

I loved teaching chemistry, and now all of you are suffering through my comments because of it.

There's a very famous story about tisanes or HERBTEA. In "A La Recherche du Temps Perdu (Remembrance of Things Past)," Marcel Proust in his multi-volume autobiography talks about a memory of his whole life when he again tastes the Madeleine biscuits dipped in tisane that he was offered as a child. This is a motif of the whole work.

From the internet:

"In Marcel Proust's novel Swann's Way, the narrator dips a madeleine cake into hot lime-blossom (linden) tisane, which triggers a powerful wave of involuntary childhood memories.

"The Literary Scene

• The Act: The adult narrator tastes a crumb of a scallop-shaped madeleine soaked in hot lime-flower tea (tisane) offered by his mother.
• The Trigger: The sensory combination instantly unlocks a forgotten memory of his Aunt Léonie giving him tea-soaked madeleines on Sunday mornings in Combray.
• The Result: This flash of memory resurrects not just a single moment, but the entire village, its houses, and gardens from his youth.

Cultural Impact

• Proust's Madeleine: The phrase la madeleine de Proust is now a common French expression for any sensory cue—a scent, taste, or sound—that instantly brings back vivid nostalgic memories."

As I remember from my double course in Proust in college, his sentences are so long that when you get to the end of the sentence, you can't remember what the beginning of the sentence was about. Even in English.

I also took a double course in Hemingway. He is the opposite--known for short sentences!
